evidence.text: Inspected the attached scan pixels. The actual headword is 一, with reading yī and phonological labels “影组、质部; 影组、质韵、於悉切.” The entry calls it a 指事字, says the ancient graphs 一 through 四 use one to four horizontal strokes as primitive counting symbols, and identifies its basic meaning as the smallest positive integer. It cites 玉篇 and 尚書《洪範》 for “one as the beginning of number” and ordinal use. It says that from the Spring and Autumn/Warring States period 一 could be written with added strokes/components as elaborated forms, analogous to forms of 二 and 三, and that these spellings later fell out of use. This paraphrase relies on the scan-verified claims, not an emendation of its printed forms.

evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析 — 一; historical explanation and oracle-bone uses
evidence.text: The entry says oracle and bronze forms, as well as small seal, use a horizontal stroke for the number one. It records oracle-bone uses as a numeral in 《合集》21575「一牛」 and ordinal “first” in 《合集》2703「今一月」, and also gives the usage 《合集》41027「余一人亡(無)𡆥(憂)」. It does not supply an absolute date for those cited inscriptions on this page. Its discussion of 弌 is separate from the basic 一 graph: it reports a traditional Shuowen label 古文一 and describes later competing or tentative analyses of the added form.

evidence.source: 古代漢字研究 — 漢数字の起源
evidence.field: 第一章「一から四の起源」, section 1, paragraphs 154–180
evidence.text: This scholarly discussion presents several accounts for 一 through 四: a count of extended fingers, counting rods, or an abstract indicative mark for the imagined number. It describes the one-line indicative account as drawing quantity one with a single line, but concludes that the exact route (direct mark versus mediation by fingers or rods) cannot be decided on the evidence discussed. Its author favors 指事 as a general precursor, while acknowledging uncertainty about the concrete graphic process. This is a modern study's analysis, not direct proof of a specific depicted object.
evidence.title: 古代漢字研究 ―漢数字の起源―

evidence.text: The page lists examples labeled oracle bone, bronze, Warring States, seal, Shuowen ancient form, clerical and regular script. It also treats the elaborated 弌 form as a device to make numeral marks less easy to alter.
